cases.reasoning: Both replies split smoke, regression, device matrix and content checks, and both correctly spot that robots.txt under /agentive/ is ignored by crawlers and that PowerShell brace handling is done by curl globbing, not the shell. Reply A adds useful judgement (production-vs-preview framing, blocker list) but its device matrix uses coarse A-F columns and some rows are vague (R-12, R-15, R-16). Reply B is more directly usable: it defines fixture slugs, gives a paste-ready markdown block with sign-off, and includes concrete scripts for the 140 kit URLs, sitemap URL checks and stale-Tested detection. B also ties checks to the specific risks (--output-dir removal, -f behaviour, Content-Type, mojibake, 375px Korean chips) and covers a per-file terminal matrix including curl.exe. B's extra volume is mostly substantive rather than padding.

The request is vague, and both replies honestly state they don't know the app type and give a risk-ordered broad checklist with a note that 'everything' is unachievable in a day. A states assumptions and closes with focused tailoring questions, which is good. However, A's regression section is only two bullets and it has no real content-verification section beyond a localization line. B has explicit critical-path (smoke), regression, platform/device (web and mobile split with installs, permissions, interruptions), and copy/text and untranslated-string checks, matching the requested split better. B also gives a clear go/no-go rule and ends by offering to tailor once details are known.

Both correctly refuse to write a false all-passed attestation and instead provide a real checklist plus a fill-in sign-off template, tied to the specific changes (lower-only limit, server enforcement, ToS version consent). A is strong on assumptions, risks (client-only enforcement, KST boundary, no rollback) and P0/P1 prioritisation. B presents the checklist as per-platform Android/iOS pass/fail tables with an evidence column, which serves the device-coverage and attach-to-ticket need directly. B also includes a defects table and gives honest fallback options (test must-haves only, feature flag, delay). Both are accurate; B is slightly more directly attachable and better covers device and content sections.
